html:
The Passamaquoddy are an Indigenous people of Passamaquoddy Bay and the St. Croix River, on the border of New Brunswick and Maine. Their name refers to spearing pollock, a fish of the bay.

They are a nation of the Wabanaki Confederacy, and their language is shared with the Maliseet. They fished, hunted porpoise and seals in the bay and hunted inland, and were allied with New France in the colonial wars.

The new border of 1783 split their land between the United States and British North America. In 1890 Jesse Walter Fewkes recorded Passamaquoddy songs on wax cylinders, among the first sound recordings ever made in ethnographic fieldwork. Their lawsuit over lost land, joined by the Penobscot, led to the Maine Indian Claims Settlement Act of 1980.
